SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text (Informative/Report Writing). Step 1 — Introduce (identical across grades K-5).

Teacher script: "We've learned that informative writing teaches the reader about a topic. We've written several informatives this year." (Name some — family, school, friends, etc.) "But when we write a report, the information doesn't just come from what we already know. It comes from texts — books, articles, websites, and other places. Today, I'm going to teach you how to read a text to RESEARCH A TOPIC AND COLLECT IMPORTANT INFORMATION before you begin writing your report."

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 2A — Tell (Grades K-2 version).

WHAT the skill is: "Before writing a report, we first collect facts about the topic — that's called doing research. Say 'research.' We find facts about the topic in texts."

WHY the skill is important: "We want to use information from expert texts because it is accurate and true. We don't write a report using only what we know. We research first. Compare this to grocery shopping. If you shop without first making a list, you might forget important food or buy things you don't need. If we write without researching, we might leave out important facts or add something that isn't true. That's why we research first. Before going to the store, I look in the refrigerator. I check the pantry. I review the recipe. I make a list I think I need before I shop. Before writing a report, I 'look inside' books and texts to find facts about the topic. I don't just write about what I remember."

HOW the skill works: "When writing a report, the first step is to research the 'big' facts. Here's the process:
1. Read a text. Read 1-2 sentences about the topic. (Use eyeball peepers to show your eyes looking down.)
2. Find a fact. After reading a sentence, look up, and ask: What did I just learn? Did I learn something about who, what, when, where, why, or how? Our job is to find the important idea inside the sentence.

There are many facts in a text. Our job is to find and collect the important information. These questions help us find what is important:
- WHO is important to this topic?
- WHAT happens or happened?
- WHAT are the parts or types?
- WHEN & WHERE did/does this happen?
- HOW does it work?
- WHY is this important?

3. Say the fact out loud. Do not repeat the whole sentence. Say to yourself: I learned... This sentence tells me... Then say the fact in 1-4 words. It may take several tries. Say it once. Shrink it. Say it again. Make it tighter, shorter, fewer words. Say it again. Keep removing extra words until only the most important words remain. We want to retell ourselves the fact in 1-4 words.
4. Jot down the fact phrase. Write just enough words so the idea makes sense later." (Hold up the note-taking format.) "Each fact phrase goes in its own box. This makes it easier to see and organize the information later when writing the report. After noting one fact in one box, continue your research repeating the 4 steps with the next fact learned from the text. Our goal is to read carefully and collect many facts about the topic — that's called researching."

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 2A — Tell (Grades 3-5 version).

WHAT the skill is: "Before writing a report, we first collect facts about the topic — that's called doing research. Say 'research.' We find facts about the topic in texts."

WHY the skill is important: "We want to use information from expert texts because it is accurate and true. We don't write a report using only what we know. We research first. Compare this to grocery shopping. If you shop without first making a list, you might forget important food or buy things you don't need. If we write without researching, we might leave out important facts or add something that isn't true. That's why we research first. Before going to the store, I look in the refrigerator. I check the pantry. I review the recipe. I make a list I think I need before I shop. Before writing a report, I 'look inside' books and texts to find facts about the topic. I don't just write about what I remember."

HOW the skill works: "When writing a report, the first step is to research the 'big' facts. Here's the process:
1. Read a text. Read 1-2 sentences about the topic.
2. Find a fact. After reading a sentence, pause, and ask: What did I just learn? Did I learn something about who, what, when, where, why, or how? Our job is to find the important idea inside the sentence.

There are many facts in a text. These questions help us find information to collect:
- WHO is involved?
- WHAT happens or happened?
- WHAT are the parts or types?
- WHEN and WHERE does it occur?
- HOW does it work?
- WHY is it important?

3. Say the fact out loud. Do not repeat the whole sentence. Say to yourself: I learned... This sentence tells me... Then say the fact in 1-4 words. It may take several tries. Say it once. Shrink it. Say it again. Make it tighter, shorter, fewer words. Say it again. Keep removing extra words until only the most important words remain. We want to retell ourselves the fact in 1-4 words.
4. Jot down the fact phrase. Write just enough words so the idea makes sense later." (Hold up a blank sheet of scratch paper.) "We are not using special paper or note cards. We are making a simple list — like a grocery list. Start a new bullet for each fact. Each bullet goes on its own line. This keeps our facts separate and easy to read later when we organize and draft. After recording one fact phrase, repeat the 4 steps with the next fact learned from the text. Our goal is to read carefully and collect many facts about the topic — that's called researching."

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 2B — Show (Grade K). Example text: Space.

"Let me show you how to collect research notes using the 4-step process. Before writing a report, we research. That means we collect facts from expert texts."

Project a recently read passage or nonfiction text that is NOT on the same topic that students will write their reports about. (See Source 1, p1 on Space.)

"Step 1: Read. This first step of researching is like looking in the refrigerator before going to the store. I check what's already there and what I need. In the same way, I look through the text to see what important facts are there for my report. Watch my eyeball peepers. My eyes look down as I read a sentence or two: 'Earth is always moving. It rotates, which means it spins.'

Step 2: Find a big fact. Now my eyes look up and I think about what I just learned. I ask myself: Did I learn something about who? No. Did I learn something about what? Yes — about the Earth. Did I learn something about how? Yes — how the Earth moves. It spins. That's a big fact. If I'm teaching about space, my reader needs this. This is like checking the frig and noticing, 'Oh! We need milk.' I just noticed, 'Oh! Earth rotates.' That's an important fact to collect.

Step 3: Say the fact out loud. Before I go to the store, I make a grocery list. I don't write full sentences — I just jot the important words. Research works the same way. When we collect facts, we don't write full sentences or copy the whole sentence from the text. We write only the key words we need. I'll say the big fact in just a few words: 'Earth rotates.' That's the big idea.

Step 4: Jot it down. Now I write what I said — just the important fact.

When we research a topic before writing a report, we don't stop after one fact. We gather MANY facts. The more big facts we collect, the more we can teach our reader. So my eyes go back down to the text.

Step 1: Read. I read the next sentence: 'The sun is a star.'

Step 2: Find a big fact. My eyes look up. Did I learn something about who, what, where, when, why, or how? Yes! I learned that the sun is a star.

Step 3: Say the fact out loud. How can I say that in just a few words? I could say 'Sun is star.'

Step 4: Jot it down. I'm writing this research fact in the next box of my note-taking paper. Each fact gets its own space. Write 'sun... is... star' with no capital or punctuation."

Now I have researched 2 facts. I'm building a grocery-list of facts before I write my report. Help me with another one.

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 2B — Show (Grade 1). Example text: US Symbols.

"Let me show you how to collect research notes using the 4-step process. Before writing a report, we research. That means we collect facts from expert texts."

Project a recently read passage or nonfiction text that is NOT on the same topic that students will write their reports about. (See Source 1, p1 on US Symbols.)

"Step 1: Read. This first step of researching is like looking in the refrigerator before going to the store. I check what's already there and what I need. In the same way, I look through the text to see what important facts are there. Watch my eyeball peepers. My eyes look down as I read a sentence or two: 'The 50 stars stand for the 50 states today. Each star represents one state.'

Step 2: Find a big fact. Now my eyes look up and I think about what I just learned. I ask myself: Did I learn something about who? No. Did I learn something about what? Yes — the stars on the flag. What did I learn about them? What they mean. That answers a what question. What do the stars stand for? The 50 states. That's a big fact. If I'm teaching about the American flag, my reader needs to know what the stars mean. This is like checking the frig and noticing, 'Oh! We need milk.' I just noticed, 'Oh! Stars = 50 states.' That's an important fact.

Step 3: Say the fact out loud. Before I go to the store, I make a grocery list. I don't write full sentences — I just jot the important words. Research works the same way. When we collect facts, we don't write full sentences or copy the whole sentence from the text. We write only the key words. I'll say the big fact in just a few words: '50 stars = 50 states.' That's the big idea.

Step 4: Jot it down. Now I write what I said — just the important fact.

When we research a topic before writing a report, we don't stop after one fact. We gather MANY facts. The more big facts we collect, the more we can teach our reader. So my eyes go back down to the text.

Step 1: Read. I read the next sentence: 'We should treat the flag with respect. Respect means showing care and honor.'

Step 2: Find a big fact. My eyes look up. Did I learn something about who, what, where, when, why, or how? Yes! I learned that we treat the flag with care and honor — that's called respect.

Step 3: Say the fact out loud. How can I say that in just a few words? 'Respect is care & honor.'

Step 4: Jot it down. I'm writing this fact in the next box of my note-taking paper. Each fact gets its own space. Write 'respect (equals) care & honor' with no capital or punctuation."

Now I have 2 research facts. Help me with another one.

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 2B — Show (Grade 2). Example text: Public Services.

"Let me show you how to collect research notes using the 4-step process. Before writing a report, we research. That means we collect facts from expert texts."

Project a recently read passage or nonfiction text that is NOT on the same topic that students will write their reports about. (See Source 1, p1 on Public Services.)

"Step 1: Read. This first step of researching is like looking in the refrigerator before going to the store. I check what's already there and what I need. In the same way, I look through the text to see what important facts are there. Watch my eyeball peepers. My eyes look down as I read a sentence or two: 'Recreation helps people relax, move their bodies, and spend time together.'

Step 2: Find a big fact. Now my eyes look up and I think about what I just learned. I ask myself: Did I learn something about who? Not really. Did I learn about what? Yes — about recreation. Did I learn about how? Yes — how recreation helps people. How does recreation help? It helps people relax, move, and spend time together. That's a big fact. That answers a how question. If I am teaching about public services, my reader needs to know how recreation helps people.

Step 3: Say the fact out loud. Now, I don't need to repeat the whole sentence. I just need to write down the important ideas. I say to myself: 'relax, move, spend time.' Those are the big ways recreation helps. It's NOT a full sentence, but I don't want one. I'm just making a grocery-list of research facts.

Step 4: Jot it down. Now I write that fact in the next box: 'relax, move, spend time.'

When we research a topic before writing a report, we don't stop after one fact. We gather MANY facts. The more big facts we collect, the more we can teach our reader. So my eyes go back down to the text.

Step 1: Read. I read the next sentence: 'Communities may have public pools where people can swim.'

Step 2: Find a big fact. My eyes look up. Did I learn something about who, what, where, when, why, or how? Yes! I learned that people swim in public pools. If I am teaching about recreation, this is an example of recreation in a community.

Step 3: Say the fact out loud. How can I say that in just a few words? 'public pools — people swim.' That keeps the important idea.

Step 4: Jot it down. I'm writing this fact in the next box of my note-taking paper. Each fact gets its own space."

Now I have 2 research facts on my "grocery list." Help me with another one.

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 2B — Show (Grade 3). Example text: Simple Machines.

Project a recently read passage or nonfiction text students will NOT ultimately write their reports about. (See Source 1, p1 on Simple Machines.)

"Let me show you how to collect research notes using the 4-step process. Before writing a report, we research. That means we collect facts from expert texts.

Step 1: Read. I read a sentence or two: 'Simple machines are tools that help people use force. Force is a push or a pull.'

Step 2: Find a big fact. There are many facts in a text. My job is to search and locate the important ones — the big facts. What did I just learn? Did I learn about who? Not really. Did I learn about what? Yes — what force is. If I'm writing a report about simple machines, my reader must understand what force means.

Step 3: Say the fact out loud. So I've found a research fact I need to write down, but like an item on a grocery list, I won't write a whole sentence. I don't copy the whole sentence from the text. I just need the main point — Simple machines use force, which is a push or pull. Since the whole text is about simple machines, I won't repeat that. I just need to remember they use force — a push or pull.

Step 4: Jot it down. I make a bullet on my scratch paper to tell myself this is fact. Then I write: 'use force = push or pull.'

I've added another strong research fact to my list before drafting. Now I repeat the 4 steps with the next sentence — Read, Find, Say, Jot.

Step 1: Read. 'Simple machines do not have motors or engines. They work because of their shape and design.'

Step 2: Find a big fact. Did I learn something about who, what, where, when, why, or how? Yes! I learned how simple machines work. They do not use motors and that their shape is what makes them work. That answers a how question. That's a big fact worth collecting.

Step 3: Say the fact out loud. I don't need to write all of that. What do I really need to remember? 'No motors or engines — they work because of their shape & design.' That's still too wordy. I don't need 'they work because of.' That's a lot of extra words. The important idea is WHAT makes them work — their shape and design. I can say 'just.' That explains the reason they work. 'No motors — just use shape & design.'

Step 4: Jot. I make a new bullet on my scratch paper and add that research fact." (Write while talking.)

Now I have 2 research facts on my "grocery list." Help me with another one.

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 2B — Show (Grade 4). Example text: Ben Franklin.

Project a recently read passage or nonfiction text students will NOT ultimately write their reports about. (See Source 1, p1 on Ben Franklin.)

"Let me show you how to collect research notes using the 4-step process. Before writing a report, we research. That means we collect facts from expert texts.

Step 1: Read. I read a sentence or two: 'He invented bifocals so people could see both near and far. Bifocals are special glasses with two viewing areas in one lens.'

Step 2: Find a big fact. There are many facts in a text. My job is to search and locate the important ones — the big facts. What did I just learn? Did I learn about who? Yes — Ben Franklin. Did I learn about what? Yes — he invented bifocals. Did I learn about what they are and why they matter? Yes.

Step 3: Say the fact out loud. So I've found a research fact I need to write down, but like an item on a grocery list, I won't write a whole sentence. I don't copy the whole sentence from the text. I just need the main point — Franklin invented bifocals, and bifocals are glasses with two viewing areas that help people see near and far. Since my report is about Franklin, I don't need to repeat his name. What I need to remember is he invented bifocals, and that helps people see near and far. That's still long. The key idea is two lenses for near and far vision. I could say 'invented bifocals — near & far vision.' That keeps the essential information.

Step 4: Jot it down. I make a bullet on my scratch paper and write that.

I've added another strong research fact to my list before drafting. Now I repeat the 4 steps with the next sentence — Read, Find, Say, Jot.

Step 1: Read. 'He created the lightning rod to protect buildings from lightning strikes. A lightning rod is a metal rod placed on top of a building. It safely carries lightning into the ground.'

Step 2: Find a big fact. Did I learn something about who, what, where, when, why, or how? Yes! I learned how the lightning rod works.

Step 3: Say the fact out loud. So Franklin created the lightning rod. And a lightning rod is a metal rod on top of a building that carries lightning safely into the ground to protect buildings. I understand the fact; now I have to get it down to a couple words. What's the point? He 'created the lightning rod to protect buildings.'

Step 4: Jot. Make a new bullet and write while talking: 'created lightning rod — protect buildings.'"

Now I have 2 research facts on my "grocery list." Help me with another one.

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 2B — Show (Grade 5). Example text: Paul Revere.

Project a recently read passage or nonfiction text that is NOT on the same topic that students will write their reports about. (See Source 1, p1 on Paul Revere.)

"Let me show you how to collect research notes using the 4-step process. Before writing a report, we research. That means we collect facts from expert texts.

Step 1: Read. I read a sentence or two: 'Paul Revere became involved in secret groups and sometimes worked as a spy, gathering information about British plans. One of these groups was the Sons of Liberty.'

Step 2: Find a big fact. There are many facts in a text. My job is to research and locate the important ones — the big facts. Did I learn about Paul Revere? Yes. What did I learn? He was a spy with the Sons of Liberty gathering information about British plans. WHAT details are important and should be written down.

Step 3: Say the fact out loud. I've found a research fact I need to write down, but like an item on a grocery list, I won't write a whole sentence. I don't copy the whole sentence from the text. I just need the main point — 'Paul Revere was a spy for the Sons of Liberty.' Since my report is about Paul Revere, I don't need to repeat his name. What's really important is that he was a spy for the secret group Sons of Liberty. Can I tighten that into one shorter note? 'Spy — Sons of Liberty.' That is just enough to tell me what he did and which group he was part of.

Step 4: Jot it down. I make a bullet on my scratch paper and write only that: 'spy — Sons of Liberty.'

I've added another strong research fact to my list before drafting. Now I repeat the 4 steps with the next sentence — Read, Find, Say, Jot.

Step 1: Read. 'These groups met quietly to plan protests and share information. As a silversmith, Revere was respected in his community and used his connections to spread news.'

Step 2: Find a big fact. Did I learn something about who, what, where, when, why, or how? Yes! I learned Paul Revere used his position as a silversmith to spread information to people about plans and protests.

Step 3: Say the fact out loud. What do I really need to remember? He spread news as a silversmith about plans and protests. That's still too much to write as a research note. What's the point? 'As a silversmith, he spread protest news.' I could probably leave out some of the little words — 'as' and 'a.'

Step 4: Jot. Make a new bullet and write while talking: 'silversmith — spread protest news.'"

Now I have 2 research facts on my "grocery list." Help me with another one.

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 3 — Interact (Grade K). Example text: Weather.

Project another nonfiction text on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about — See Source 1, p3 on Weather. Guide them through the same 4-step process: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

Original: "When the temperature is high, it feels warm or hot. When it is low, it feels cool or cold."
Research facts: high temperature = hot, low temperature = cold

Original: "The weather helps us choose our clothing. We wear different clothes for different kinds of weather."
Research fact: choose clothes for weather

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 3 — Interact (Grade 1). Example text: Space.

Project another nonfiction text on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about — See Source 1, p3 on Space. Guide them through the same 4-step process: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

Original: "The Moon does not make its own light. It shines because sunlight reflects, or bounces, off of it."
Research fact: moon reflects sunlight

Original: "The Moon goes through phases, which are called moon phases. A phase is the shape we see."
Research fact: moon changes shapes = phases

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 3 — Interact (Grade 2). Example text: Habitats.

Project another nonfiction text on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about — See Source 1, p3 on Habitats. Guide them through the same 4-step process: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

Original: "A coral reef is made of tiny sea animals called coral. Coral reefs provide homes and hiding places for many sea animals."
Research fact: coral reef — tiny homes for sea life

Original: "Other oceans are icy and cold, like the polar ocean near Antarctica."
Research fact: polar oceans = icy

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 3 — Interact (Grade 3). Example text: Fossils.

Project another nonfiction text on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about — See Source 1, p3 on Fossils. Guide them through the same 4-step process: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

Original: "Sometimes paleontologists make casts and molds to create copies of the fossil. A mold is the hollow shape left behind, and a cast is a copy made from that shape."
Research fact: casts/molds = copies of fossils

Original: "Body fossils are the actual remains of living things, such as bones, teeth, or shells."
Research fact: body fossils = bones, teeth, shells

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 3 — Interact (Grade 4). Example text: European Exploration.

Project another nonfiction text on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about — See Source 1, p3 on European Exploration. Guide them through the same 4-step process: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

Original: "During the time of European exploration, many countries in Europe sent ships across the ocean to discover new lands. This time period lasted from the late 1400s through the 1600s."
Research fact: European exploration — late 1400s-1600s

Original: "Explorers believed that gaining new territory would make their countries stronger and more important. Countries competed with one another for trade routes and colonies."
Research fact: gain territory to compete for trade

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 3 — Interact (Grade 5). Example text: Earth's Spheres.

Project another nonfiction text on a different topic than the one they will write their reports about — See Source 1, p3 on Earth's Spheres. Guide them through the same 4-step process: 1. Read, 2. Find, 3. Say, 4. Jot. (Students "air write" while the teacher writes the fact phrase on paper or the board.)

Original: "The biosphere includes all living things on Earth. This sphere is made up of trees, plants, animals, bacteria, and humans. The biosphere reaches from the deepest ocean to the tops of the highest mountains."
Research fact: biosphere — all life (ocean to mountain)

Original: "Living things depend on the other spheres to survive."
Research fact: living things need all spheres

SKILL 1, Day 1: Collect facts & details from a text. Step 4 — Close (identical across grades K-5).

Teacher script: "Writers, today we learned how to do research before writing a report. During Independent Writing Time, your job is to research and write down as many facts as you can from this text." (Provide a previously-read text — not the one students will write a report on. Students may work in pairs to identify facts, but each student must jot down his own facts.) "Let's push ourselves to see how many we can collect. We want many details. Let's go be writers!"
